items.title: Agents that work for you, and agents that visit: two kinds of agent readiness
items.desc: Some AI agents work on your site for you. Others visit it for someone else. Here's how the two kinds of agent readiness differ, where they overlap, and how to prepare for both.
items.full: Loading... In my last post , I looked at WebMCP, which lets a site offer actions to AI agents that are accessing a site alongside a visitor in the browser. That post, like the two before it, was about one angle of agent readiness: getting your site ready for agents that visit it on someone else’s behalf. But there’s also a second kind of agent readiness related to the agents that do work for you on your site. The two often get mixed up since they’re both referred to as related to “agent readiness,” and they both often involve something called MCP. In this post I’ll look at how the two are different, and where they overlap. By the way, if you’re new to this series, the first post covers what agent-ready means. Let’s look at a small bakery that sells cakes through its WordPress site: on Monday morning, the owner asks Claude to write descriptions for three new cakes and add them to the shop as drafts. That afternoon, a customer asks the AI assistant in their browser to find a chocolate cake that serves 12 and can be picked up on Friday, and the assistant searches the bakery’s site and adds one to the cart. Both of these are AI agents using the same “agent-ready” site, but they’re coming from different directions, working for different people, and they have different abilities. The owner’s agent works for, and on, the site. It was purposefully connected, and signs in as the owner, which gives it the ability to change things. The customer’s agent works for the visitor: it doesn’t have a pre-configured connection, it probably isn’t signed in at all, and it can only do whatever the site allows all public visitors to do. This is the kind of agent readiness many WordPress site owners have already run into, even if they didn’t call it that. You, someone on your team, or an agency you work with connects an AI assistant like Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor to your site, and then uses it for real work, like writing and editing posts, building pages, changing settings, or pulling reports. The connection usually goes through MCP, which I covered in my post on what agents actually use . In WordPress, the MCP Adapter plugin turns what the site can do into MCP tools, served from the site itself, so the assistant can connect directly to your site. The Elementor MCP does this for Elementor sites: an admin picks their preferred AI tool in the Elementor area of the WordPress dashboard, and follows the steps to connect it to their site. Once that’s done, the assistant can build pages in Elementor’s own structure, saving each one as a draft for you to review before it goes live. (To avoid confusion, Angie is an AI agent that works from within your site, so you don’t have to connect an outside assistant when using it.) Because this kind of agent can change things, it has to sign in to get the relevant permissions. Since WordPress 5.6, Application Passwords let you give an app its own password, tied to a user account, which you can revoke later without touching your main login. The Elementor MCP creates one for you in the background when you connect. Once it’s signed in, the agent can do whatever that user’s role allows. Setting up an MCP server like this is a one-time job

items.title: Microsoft details how state-backed hackers use the ARTEX AI framework to automate cyberattacks
items.desc: Microsoft has published the technical architecture of ARTEX, an AI framework in wide use since July 2026 that runs cyberattacks with specialized agents and almost no human involvement. State-backed groups from China and North Korea, along with criminal organizations, are already using the system. Microsoft recommends deception techniques like honeypots and faked success signals as defenses, but how long those will hold up against agents that learn and adapt remains an open question. The article Microsoft details how state-backed hackers use the ARTEX AI framework to automate cyberattacks appea
items.full: The AI framework ARTEX automates cyberattacks from reconnaissance to data theft. A Microsoft analysis shows how state-backed groups and cybercriminals use its specialized agents at machine speed, and how defenders can respond. Since its release in July 2026, the AI-powered penetration-testing framework ARTEX has become a go-to tool for cyberattacks. The software was recently suspected of being used in an intrusion into an analytics system run by the CIA, NGA, and ODNI (Link nicht geprüft). That breach surfaced shortly before US financial crimes agency FinCEN reported a security incident. The FBI and the US Department of Agriculture had reported incidents earlier. A report from Microsoft Threat Intelligence now details how ARTEX works and how widely it has spread. GitHub user "Autumn-27" published the source code in July and deleted it in October, though other developers still distribute copies. Chinese security firm ThreatBook also sells a commercial Pro version. Microsoft says state-backed groups from China and North Korea have integrated ARTEX into their operations, including Salt Typhoon, Crystal Typhoon, Onyx Sleet, and Storm-0940 . Financially motivated cybercriminals also use the system, the company says, with both state-backed and criminal groups deploying it in operations such as supply chain attacks. Microsoft points out that ARTEX doesn't invent new attack techniques. Instead, the framework operates existing security software with almost no human intervention, including tools such as Nmap, Sqlmap, Metasploit, and automated headless browsers. Attackers can connect any large language model, including modified versions without safety guardrails. A built-in pooling feature automatically switches models or API keys on errors or usage limits, making attacks hard for any single AI provider to track. According to Microsoft, the system is built on a multi-agent architecture. A goal model breaks an attacker's instructions into verifiable subgoals. From there, a planning agent continuously reviews a knowledge graph, a dynamic map of discovered systems and vulnerabilities, to assign short attack tasks. Worker agents carry out those tasks via system commands, including deploying web shells on web servers, reading password files, or hijacking cloud accounts. Each new finding feeds back into the map and prompts the planning agent for the next step until a reporting agent documents all exploited flaws. Automation cuts defender response times to just a few minutes, the company found. In one case, an AI agent took just five minutes to search for accidentally exposed credentials on GitHub and pull data from Azure Key Vault, a cloud key store. During a Storm-0940 campaign, the company logged more than 151,000 failed login attempts from automated password guessing, peaking at 2,900 per minute. In that same campaign, Microsoft observed some compromised apps granting themselves top administrator privileges. Conventional rule-based filters often fail against ARTEX because they rely on fixed markers like known IP addresses or the browser identifiers "artex-enrich" and "norma." items.title: Nvidia halts server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia after tighter US export controls
items.desc: Nvidia has told partners such as Dell and Supermicro to stop shipping servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia. Following new US export controls targeting Chinese cloud access, dealers are already seeking buyers for thousands of B300 chips, while one cloud executive describes "chaos", Loans and major deals are now on the line for Southeast Asia's data centers. The article Nvidia halts server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia after tighter US export controls appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: The US is closing cloud loopholes that give Chinese companies access to AI chips. Nvidia is responding by halting shipments to four countries, while thousands of high-performance processors are looking for new buyers on the secondary market. Nvidia has told manufacturing partners such as Dell and Supermicro to stop shipping servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia. The Financial Times reported the halt, citing three people familiar with the matter. It isn't clear whether the pause is only temporary, according to the report. The move follows tighter US export controls from the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security. The rules aim to stop Chinese companies from getting around existing sales bans by renting computing power from foreign cloud providers. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC the goal was to block indirect access, including smuggling through Southeast Asia and remote access via data centers in third countries. Ad The controls are already affecting the hardware market, CNBC reported. Since the announcement, dealers have listed an unusually large number of Nvidia GPUs for sale. Jack Duhamel, president of the AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two other insiders confirmed to CNBC that the surge is a direct result of the new rule. According to the report, sellers are looking for new buyers for hardware, including thousands of B300 chips, one of Nvidia's most advanced models. Those chips were originally intended for data centers with Chinese rental customers. Ad The rollout has created significant uncertainty in Southeast Asia, the Financial Times reported. Cloud providers have 90 days to apply for a license and prove that no restricted companies are among their end users. One cloud provider executive described the situation to the paper as chaos, saying there was no guidance on how to apply. The fallout is also hitting major infrastructure projects. Banks have halted about $500 million in loans to Singapore-based cloud provider Aolani, which planned to rent computing power to TikTok parent ByteDance, the Financial Times reported. ByteDance could now pull out of the deal. Ad Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.title: US chip-access curbs and anti-distillation measures are reportedly already slowing Chinese AI labs
items.desc: Chip restrictions, anti-distillation measures, and shrinking access to Nvidia hardware abroad are putting growing pressure on Deepseek, Moonshot AI, and Alibaba, according to a report. Deepseek researchers internally estimate they're already up to nine months behind US models, and the gap is widening. The article US chip-access curbs and anti-distillation measures are reportedly already slowing Chinese AI labs appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: The US is tightening its grip in the AI race with China, and the push is already having an effect, according to The Information. Chinese AI developers including Deepseek, Moonshot AI, and Alibaba have been under pressure since September, squeezed by restrictions on Chinese firms' remote access to advanced Nvidia chips in foreign data centers and by successful anti-distillation measures from OpenAI and Anthropic . As a result, many ongoing projects are facing delays, the report says . Last month, Deepseek researchers internally estimated that their gap to top US models could grow from three to six months to nine months if distillation disappears completely . Moonshot AI has already canceled a $150 million deal for Nvidia Blackwell chips in Indonesia . Chinese firms are now looking for new workarounds, the publication reports. Some are trying to rent computing power through non-Chinese third parties, while companies such as MiniMax, Mihoyo, and Alibaba are leaning more heavily on domestic chips. They are also investing more in training data for their own reinforcement learning. Ad Ad Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says letting AI govern society would be "a bad idea"
items.desc: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back on an Axios report saying some employees believe humanity will hand power to superintelligent systems. Amodei says "turning over governance to AI is a bad idea." The article Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says letting AI govern society would be "a bad idea" appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Dario Amodei said it was "absurd" to suggest he believed people should "surrender human free will" to AI systems. In a lengthy post on X, he responded to an Axios report that cited people familiar with internal discussions. The outlet reported that some Anthropic employees believed humanity would safely hand authority to superintelligent systems, and often should, rather than fight for control. AI must be governed by "legitimate democratic processes," Amodei wrote . Political decisions should stay in human hands, he argued, and he rejected handing power to AI as firmly as he rejected autocracy. Ad [...] We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination on the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word to governance by AI, and I feel just as strongly that handing over governance to AI is a bad idea. Ad Automating specific tasks such as driving, developing cancer drugs, and writing software could benefit humanity, Amodei said, but that was a different matter from giving up free will in politics. End-to-end automation could also bring risks, Amodei wrote, including serious job disruption and AI building new models without human oversight. "It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives," he wrote. "But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it." In many cases, he added, "humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better." Ad Amodei said AI companies didn't differ much on automating specific tasks. Some AI CEOs, he wrote, repeated slogans like "human control and agency" and "AI should be just a tool" but still shipped products built for more and more automation. Anthropic, by contrast, refused to allow its existing models to be used for autonomous weapons during its dispute with the Pentagon . He was "willing to risk Anthropic's future as a company" over that refusal, "even in the face of legal sanctions," Amodei wrote. Ad Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.title: OpenAI wants companies to trust it with sensitive work by promising not to look at their data
items.desc: OpenAI is testing a new feature called "Private Inference" that lets companies run queries on its most powerful models without OpenAI being able to access the data. The article OpenAI wants companies to trust it with sensitive work by promising not to look at their data appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: OpenAI is testing a new feature called "Private Inference" that lets companies run queries on its most powerful models without OpenAI being able to access the data. CEO Sam Altman said the company is now piloting the previously announced offering with its first enterprise customers. Better privacy makes AI useful for a much wider range of work, Altman wrote. Shekar, the OpenAI employee leading the effort, called it a first step toward "private intelligence for everyone." OpenAI is currently scaling up the compute capacity needed to expand the offering. For now, Private Inference targets business customers, whose data OpenAI already doesn't use for training . Consumer ChatGPT conversations, by contrast, are used for training by default unless users opt out. With Private Inference, queries are processed on specially isolated hardware whose security can be independently verified, according to OpenAI . Altman also pointed to Private Safety Processing , a system that lets OpenAI scan for abuse without storing customer data. Flagged content is encrypted and stored in the customer's own cloud, and only a secured review system can read it. Google is pursuing a similar approach with Private AI Compute . items.title: Amazon and Meta are in talks to end the block on Meta's AI shopping agent Muse in Amazon's online store.
items.desc: Amazon and Meta are in talks to bring back Muse, Meta's AI shopping agent that Amazon kicked off its platform in September. The two sides are stuck on ad revenue and who gets to control search results. That matters because Amazon's ad business generates $68.6 billion a year, and Muse already commands 51 percent of all agentic shopping orders. The article Amazon and Meta are in talks to end the block on Meta's AI shopping agent Muse in Amazon's online store. appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Amazon and Meta are in talks to end the block on Meta's AI shopping agent Muse in Amazon's online store. In September, Amazon blocked Muse's access . Ad revenue and control over search results are the main sticking points in the ongoing talks, Fortune reports . Amazon worries that shopping agents like Muse could weaken its relationship with customers and bypass the ads on its platform, a business that brings in $68.6 billion a year. Andy Jassy, Amazon's CEO, said shopping through third-party agents so far hasn't been more convenient or better than going directly to a retailer, but he didn't rule out opening access. The company also offers its own agentic shopping features, which in some cases have pulled in sellers that don't sell on Amazon . It previously tried and failed to block Perplexity . Any deal would need sign-off from both CEOs, according to Fortune. Muse is Meta's most successful consumer AI product so far, with more than 10 million users in the US and Canada. Meta is already seeing gains in its Instagram ad business because Muse helps users organize saved products, which boosts conversion rates for advertisers, CNBC reports . Data from Forter Intelligence shows that Muse recently accounted for 51 percent of all agentic orders, followed by SpaceX's Grok at 24 percent and OpenAI's ChatGPT at 22 percent. items.title: Style Queries as Conditional Modifiers
items.desc: Where style queries shine is when the condition and the styles need to live in different places, or when one condition needs to affect several things at once: components that keep working, and adapt sensibly, no matter where they end up. Style Queries as Conditional Modifiers originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full:
NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. This article is adapted from a lesson in Writing Resilient CSS, the newest module in Kevin’s course, CSS Demystified . The module covers configuration options with custom properties, math functions, relative colors, :has() , style queries, and more, all put to work in practical, reusable patterns. The course is 32% off until December 2, 2026. Modifiers have been with us for a long time, often with modifier classes, but also with attribute selectors. Some common examples are things like different versions of alerts and buttons. /* BEM approach */ .button--accent { background-color: var(--clr-accent); } /* CUBECSS approach */ .toast[data-type="error"] { border-color: var(--clr-warning); } For a lot of use cases, either of those approaches work great, but when it comes to layout, a lot of the time we want the context of where the element is being used to control things. A card is a nice example of this, where we might have several versions. .card { display: grid; gap: .75rem; } .card--horizontal { grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr; } .card--compact { padding: .75rem; gap: .5rem; } The issue here is, if I’m using .card--compact , I probably want to do that for all the cards within a section. That can be annoying to apply to each card, but that’s rendered moot since most people are doing some sort of looping in a template like this these days.

And this works great, as long as we always want the cards to be compact. However, you might put this together and send it off to the design team for approval, only for them not to like that when the compact cards are lower down the page, the smaller padding isn’t needed to create visual separation between the two sections. Instead of helping with the hierarchy, it’s simply creating a strange visual inconsistency. We could use something like a resize observer to try and deal with this, but we have a better tool at our disposal: Container Style Queries , which are now Baseline Newly Available . While they all start with container , for the rest of this article I interchangeable use container query or size query for a container size query, and style query for what we’re talking about here. A quick look at style queries Before we get into the good stuff, a quick look at the basics of style queries. You’re probably familiar with size queries, which work similar to @media but look at the size of a container, rather than the viewport. Container style queries use the same @container at-rule as container size queries, but instead of looking at a size, they look at the value of a custom property. @container style(--theme: high-contrast) { .card { background: white; color: black; border-color: black; } } This reads as, “if the nearest container has --theme: high-contrast , style the .card like this.” A couple of important notes about them: Elements can’t query themselves Just like with size queries, style queries look at an ancestor , not the element itself. items.title: AI agents now control part of Deepmind's compute for Gemini experiments, but recursive self-improvement remains distant
items.desc: Google Deepmind uses AI agents to run experiments on their own for upcoming Gemini models. Research chief Koray Kavukcuoglu says the lab is still far from recursive self-improvement. For oversight, Deepmind intentionally leaves the agents' internal chains of thought untrained so they can be reviewed. Kavukcuoglu measures AGI by everyday user trust rather than benchmarks. The article AI agents now control part of Deepmind's compute for Gemini experiments, but recursive self-improvement remains distant appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Google Deepmind lets AI agents run experiments on their own for the next Gemini model. On the company's podcast, VP of Research Koray Kavukcuoglu, who leads Gemini development, frames this as part of a strategic shift at the lab. Rather than running separate teams for specialized projects like AlphaFold and nuclear fusion, Deepmind now relies on a single general-purpose algorithm for both science and products, he says. Each Gemini generation, he adds, is a hand-built one-off rather than a fixed architecture, while parallel teams work on its successors. According to Kavukcuoglu, AI agents control part of the compute themselves to run experiments, though the lab is still far from full recursive self-improvement. As a safety measure, Deepmind doesn't reward the agents' internal thought streams ("Chain of Thought") during training, he says, so their intentions stay unfiltered and reviewable in natural language before they act. Kavukcuoglu also points to limits. Today's AI can depict physical processes such as fluid flows and collisions with visual accuracy, he says, but doesn't understand them precisely. No test can show when models will close those gaps and reach artificial general intelligence (AGI), he argues, because no benchmark captures the core of intelligence. In his view, AGI won't begin until useful everyday products earn enough trust for people to hand decisions over to them, the way they would when working with other people. Ad Ad Already a subscriber? items.title: Anthropic study shows the hardest part of adopting AI at work has little to do with learning the tools
items.desc: Anthropic studied nearly 300 AI deployments across 58 US companies with sobering results. Nearly one in five still delivers no business value, held back by heavy review workloads, internal bottlenecks, and employee resistance. The researchers say the biggest hurdles stem from outdated company structures. The article Anthropic study shows the hardest part of adopting AI at work has little to do with learning the tools appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: AI models keep getting better, but putting them to work mostly creates friction, a new Anthropic report finds. Review bottlenecks, employee pushback, security risks, and outdated custom tools are dragging down many enterprise projects. Anthropic's researchers conducted 66 in-person interviews at 58 US companies for the qualitative study, from AI startups to established firms in law, construction, finance, medicine, and manufacturing. The authors note that the sample isn't representative because every participant is an Anthropic customer. Still, it offers a detailed look at nearly 300 real-world AI deployments. The findings from the "Working with AI" report amount to a reality check for anyone expecting quick efficiency gains. Respondents say 55 percent of the deployments studied produced higher output or better quality. But almost one in five (19 percent) still delivers no business value. Those deployments get stuck in internal bottlenecks (6 percent), lose their time savings to review work (5 percent), or have unclear effects (8 percent). External hurdles like regulation (4 mentions) and skeptical customers (13 mentions) barely came up. The real pain happens inside the companies themselves, according to the report. The most common obstacle cited in Anthropic's full report (PDF) is the volume of AI output that humans still need to check (49 mentions). Employee resistance (43 mentions) and required expert reviews and testing (42 mentions) rank close behind. In one case, an AI agent added one stray "S" to an API call and derailed a carefully planned software release. AI also tends to speed up only parts of a workflow while other departments fall behind (20 mentions). One industrial equipment maker found that AI could translate its product interface text into 10 languages with ease. The company shut the feature back down because nobody on staff could field customer support calls in those languages. That uneven pace breeds day-to-day conflict as power users flood coworkers with AI-generated text. The report mentions "Claude grenades" and "Claude cannons," as when an employee casually sends IT seven pages of AI-written instructions. Skeptics push back and refuse to read AI-written emails at all. One frustrated executive put it bluntly, saying, "A mediocre engineer with an AI is a menace to society." Anthropic's findings echo the broader "workslop" debate. In a survey by BetterUp Labs and the Stanford Social Media Lab , 40 percent of US workers said they regularly receive shallow AI content from colleagues. Workers spend an average of nearly two hours dealing with each incident, and the survey found that trust within teams takes a hit. Employee resistance is the second most common obstacle in Anthropic's study, with 43 mentions. Pushback is most visible when companies roll out AI from the top down to automate entire workflows. Only two of the 58 companies reported direct layoffs tied to AI automation, and five dismissed workers who refused to use AI. But the hiring impact is already visible. Both are sponsored educational partnerships developed to help freelancers and agency owners build practical skills with tools they can use in client projects. Led by instructor Ben Meredith, The WP Minute’s courses focus on practical training, real-world workflows, and tools relevant to professional WordPress work. Explore the WordPress courses hub to find more training for your agency. Email marketing is a natural extension of WooCommerce development. A store may have a well-designed website and a smooth checkout process, but it also needs ways to stay connected with customers, recover abandoned purchases, and encourage repeat orders. For agencies, understanding how to manage these activities creates opportunities to offer clients more than website development alone. The Omnisend for Agency Owners course focuses on the practical side of delivering email marketing services for WooCommerce stores. It walks through the process of connecting WooCommerce with Omnisend, creating and embedding signup forms, and configuring abandoned-cart and checkout-recovery workflows. The training also covers the technical and operational work involved in managing client accounts. This includes DNS authentication, syncing a store with a live production environment, importing contacts, organizing audience segments, and working with custom properties. Participants also learn to create campaigns, audit accounts for promotional inconsistencies, and identify broken automations that could affect customer communication. Reporting is another part of the workflow. The course demonstrates how to generate PDF analytics reports that agencies can share with clients, making it easier to communicate campaign activity and results. It also explores Omnisend’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) and how it can connect the platform with AI-powered tools such as Cursor. The course is designed for WordPress freelancers, agency owners, WooCommerce developers, and technical consultants who want to add email marketing and automation to their service offerings. The workflows can help professionals manage more of the customer journey, from collecting subscriber information to following up after a purchase. items.title: MIT team discovers that unrealistic training data makes AI climate predictions more reliable
items.desc: MIT researchers have developed a method that lets AI climate models get by with a single training run instead of the usual six to eight. An algorithm generates deliberately unrealistic scenarios with extreme CO2 or methane swings that make the model more robust. Until now, these emulators were often outdated by the time they were finished, according to the researchers. The article MIT team discovers that unrealistic training data makes AI climate predictions more reliable appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: MIT researchers have developed a method that makes training AI climate models faster, cheaper, and more reliable. According to MIT News , these emulators now need only a fraction of the data typically required. Normally, researchers rely on massive, physics-based climate simulations that take months to run a single scenario on supercomputers. Fast AI models for climate prediction can mimic these in seconds and help plan power grids, public health measures, and agriculture. But training them previously required six to eight runs of those large simulations using evenly distributed, realistic future scenarios. That took so long the finished models were usually outdated, according to co-author Noelle Selin. They also often failed on unfamiliar situations. An algorithm built by a team from MIT, ETH Zurich, and Imperial College London uses synthetic training data with extreme swings instead, like a sudden CO2 spike in 2050 or dropping methane in 2037. These targeted spikes help the AI understand the climate system far more precisely, according to lead author Christopher Womack. A single simulation run is enough for training, according to the team, and the AI reliably calculates the effects of local environmental policies too. Ad Ad Already a subscriber? Sign in
